pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew pronominal suffixes, Greek autou)
etymology: A compound of there and of, meaning of that or of it. English once had a full set of these adverbs — thereof, therein, thereon, thereto, thereby — which let a writer refer back to a thing without repeating its name. The Authorized Version uses them constantly because Hebrew does the same work with a single attached suffix.
biblical_def: Thereof means of it or belonging to it, and it is the commonest of the compound adverbs in the Authorized Version because Hebrew expresses possession by a suffix rather than a separate word. It carries the first threat in Scripture: “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” — the pronoun pointing back to the one forbidden tree without naming it again. It governs the whole sacrificial law, where the parts of an offering are distinguished with great care: “the blood thereof shall he sprinkle round about upon the altar” (Leviticus 7:2). It measures conquest by territory and its dependencies: “Judah took Gaza with the coast thereof” (Judges 1:18). And it appears in one of the great indictments of the whole earth: “The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant” (Isaiah 24:5). The word is a grammatical convenience, but the convenience is exactly what allows Scripture to speak with precision about a thing and its parts, a land and its people, a law and its penalty.
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning of that, of it, or belonging to it. In Scripture it refers back to a thing already named — the tree and eating thereof, the offering and the blood thereof, the earth and the inhabitants thereof.
webster_full: THEREOF, adv. [there and of.] Of that; of this; of it.
2. It refers to a thing or subject before mentioned, and saves the repetition of the noun.
3. It belongs to the class of compound adverbs formed with there: therein, thereon, thereto, thereby, therewith.
4. In modern usage it is retained chiefly in legal and scriptural style.
5. In Scripture, the blood thereof shall he sprinkle, Lev. 7; the inhabitants thereof, Isa. 24.
corruption_summary: Isaiah's charge that the earth is defiled under its inhabitants is now read as an environmental verdict alone, when the prophet gives the cause explicitly and it is moral: transgressed laws, a changed ordinance, a broken everlasting covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that the creation suffers under human sin, not merely under human carelessness. Isaiah 24:5 gives three causes, all of them covenantal, and Paul says the same when he writes that the creature was made subject to vanity and groaneth together until now. Christians who dismiss the state of the earth as no concern of theirs have not read the prophets; Christians who treat it as a purely technical problem have not read them either. Dominion was given to man, and a fallen steward damages what he governs.

The remedy Scripture proposes is not primarily better management but repentance and, finally, redemption — the manifestation of the sons of God, when the creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption. That hope does not license neglect in the meantime; it establishes the ground for care, since what God intends to redeem is not to be despised. The doctrine of dominion in Genesis 1 is a mandate to cultivate and keep, and the sabbath laws in Leviticus extend rest to the land itself. Both stand a long way from either indifference or the deification of nature.
roots_summary: Hebrew attaches a pronominal suffix to the noun (-o, -ah) where English needs thereof; Greek uses the genitive autou or autes; the English compound simply joins there to the preposition.
roots_lines: Hebrew suffix -o — his or its, masculine singular; the ordinary way of saying thereof.
Hebrew suffix -ah — her or its, feminine singular; used of lands and cities, which are feminine in Hebrew.
Greek autou (G846) — of him or of it; the genitive that the compound adverb renders.
Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to dwell; its participle gives the inhabitants thereof in Isaiah 24:5.
Saxon þærof — the Old English compound of there and of, source of the English word.
usage: Of the one forbidden tree, referred to without naming: in the day that thou eatest thereof (Genesis 2:17).
Of a part distinguished from the whole in sacrifice: the blood thereof shall he sprinkle round about upon the altar (Leviticus 7:2).
Of a land and the people who defile it: The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof (Isaiah 24:5).
scriptures: Leviticus 7:2
In the place where they kill the burnt offering shall they kill the trespass offering: and the blood thereof shall he sprinkle round about upon the altar.
Isaiah 24:5
The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant.
Judges 1:18
Also Judah took Gaza with the coast thereof, and Askelon with the coast thereof, and Ekron with the coast thereof.
Psalm 46:3
Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof. Selah.

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew bo and bah, Greek en auto)
etymology: A compound of there and in, meaning in that or in it. Hebrew forms it by attaching a suffix to the preposition be, in; the English compound answers to it exactly.
biblical_def: Therein means in it, and Scripture uses it above all of dwelling — who lives in a place, and on what terms. The great statement of God's title to the world runs on it: “Behold, the heaven and the heaven of heavens is the LORD'S thy God, the earth also, with all that therein is” (Deuteronomy 10:14). Everything in the world belongs to the One who made the world, and Israel's tenancy in Canaan is granted on that footing, not on conquest. Which is why the holiness laws are enforced by the land itself: “Ye shall therefore keep all my statutes, and all my judgments, and do them: that the land, whither I bring you to dwell therein, spue you not out” (Leviticus 20:22). The tenant who defiles the house is evicted, and the nations before Israel had been evicted for the same offences. The word also carries the creation mandate renewed after the flood — “be ye fruitful, and multiply; bring forth abundantly in the earth, and multiply therein” (Genesis 9:7) — and Nehemiah's note on a great city with almost nobody in it (Nehemiah 7:4).
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning in that or in it. In Scripture it is chiefly the word of dwelling — the earth and all that therein is belonging to the LORD, and the land itself spuing out tenants who will not keep His statutes.
webster_full: THEREIN, adv. [there and in.] In that; in this; in it.
2. It refers to a place, a thing, or a matter before mentioned.
3. Therein is used of place; thereinto of motion into; thereinbefore and thereinafter in legal style.
4. It answers to the Hebrew preposition be with a pronominal suffix.
5. In Scripture, the earth also, with all that therein is, Deut. 10; the land, whither I bring you to dwell therein, Lev. 20.
corruption_summary: Absolute human ownership of land and property is assumed without argument, and the tenancy Scripture describes is forgotten. The earth is the LORD's and the fulness thereof; every human title is a lease held under the Maker, on terms He set.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is creational stewardship under God's absolute title. Israel could not sell land in perpetuity, for the LORD said the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me. The jubilee returned inheritances, the gleaning laws left a margin for the poor, and the sabbath years rested the soil. None of this abolished property — the eighth commandment establishes it — but all of it qualified property as a trust.

Leviticus 20:22 adds the sanction, and it is unusually vivid: the land itself vomits out inhabitants who defile it. The Canaanites were dispossessed for the practices catalogued in that chapter, and Israel is warned in the same breath that the land will not treat her differently. This is a standing rebuke to any nation that assumes its tenure is secure because its title is old. Possession in Scripture is always conditional upon obedience, and the conditions are not secret.
roots_summary: Hebrew forms therein by suffixing the preposition be (in) — bo, in it; bah, in her. Greek uses en auto. The verb yashab, to dwell, and qi', to vomit, govern the key texts.
roots_lines: Hebrew be with suffix (bo, bah) — in it; the exact equivalent of the English compound.
Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to dwell, to sit, to remain; the verb of tenancy in the land.
Hebrew qi' (H6958) — to vomit or spue out; the land's action against defiling inhabitants in Leviticus 20:22.
Hebrew melo' (H4393) — fulness, that which fills; the earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof.
Greek en auto (G1722, G846) — in it or in him; the Greek construction behind the English adverb.
usage: Of God's absolute title to the world and its contents: the earth also, with all that therein is (Deuteronomy 10:14).
Of a land that evicts tenants who defile it: that the land, whither I bring you to dwell therein, spue you not out (Leviticus 20:22).
Of the creation mandate renewed after the flood: bring forth abundantly in the earth, and multiply therein (Genesis 9:7).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 10:14
Behold, the heaven and the heaven of heavens is the LORD'S thy God, the earth also, with all that therein is.
Leviticus 20:22
Ye shall therefore keep all my statutes, and all my judgments, and do them: that the land, whither I bring you to dwell therein, spue you not out.
Genesis 9:7
And you, be ye fruitful, and multiply; bring forth abundantly in the earth, and multiply therein.
Nehemiah 7:4
Now the city was large and great: but the people were few therein, and the houses were not builded.

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew 'alav, Greek ep' auto)
etymology: A compound of there and on, meaning on that or upon it. It answers to Hebrew 'alav, the preposition 'al with a suffix, and belongs largely to the language of altars, tabernacle furniture, and what is set upon them.
biblical_def: Thereon means upon it, and it is a word of the sanctuary. Jacob raises the first memorial pillar at Bethel and consecrates it twice over: “he poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon” (Genesis 35:14). At the completion of the tabernacle the glory settles on it so heavily that the mediator cannot enter: “Moses was not able to enter into the tent of the congregation, because the cloud abode thereon” (Exodus 40:35). Manasseh, restored from Babylon and repentant, repairs what he had torn down and offers “thereon peace offerings and thank offerings” (2 Chronicles 33:16) — one of Scripture's clearest cases of a late and genuine repentance in a wicked king. And the Lord uses the word to close a rabbinic loophole: men had distinguished swearing by the altar from swearing by the gift on the altar, and He answers that “Whoso therefore shall swear by the altar, sweareth by it, and by all things thereon” (Matthew 23:20). What rests upon a holy thing is not separable from it.
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning on that or upon it. In Scripture it belongs to the sanctuary — oil poured on a pillar, the cloud abiding on the tabernacle, offerings laid on a repaired altar, and everything that rests upon the altar sharing its holiness.
webster_full: THEREON, adv. [there and on.] On that; on this; upon it.
2. It refers to a thing before mentioned, and answers to the Hebrew 'alav.
3. Thereupon differs in expressing consequence or immediate succession, as well as position.
4. It is retained chiefly in the legal and scriptural style.
5. In Scripture, he poured a drink offering thereon, Gen. 35; the cloud abode thereon, Exo. 40.
corruption_summary: The instinct Christ rebukes in Matthew 23 — grading oaths by their object so that some may be quietly broken — survives wherever men make promises with a mental reservation, and wherever holy things are treated as detachable from the God who claims them.
corruption_paragraphs: The scribal system Christ dismantles was ingenious: an oath by the temple was nothing, but an oath by the gold of the temple was binding; an oath by the altar was nothing, but by the gift on the altar was binding. The effect, as He says, was to make men debtors when they wished to be and free when they did not. He answers by refusing the division — he that swears by the altar swears by all things thereon, and by Him that dwelleth in the house. The principle reaches every kind of fine print offered in the place of plain honesty. Let your communication be Yea, yea; Nay, nay.

The second half of the rebuke matters as much. Christ does not merely say that the greater oath includes the lesser; He says that the altar sanctifies the gift, reversing the value the scribes had assigned. What makes a thing holy is not its market worth but its relation to God. Manasseh's repaired altar in 2 Chronicles 33 makes the same point from the other direction: a king who had filled Jerusalem with idols is received when he humbles himself greatly before the God of his fathers, and what he lays thereon is accepted. Holiness runs from God outward, never from the gift inward.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'al with a suffix ('alav, upon it) is the standard form; Greek uses epi with the dative or genitive. The sanctuary vocabulary — mizbeach, altar; matstsebah, pillar — supplies the setting.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'alav (H5921) — upon it or upon him; the preposition 'al with a pronominal suffix.
Hebrew matstsebah (H4676) — a standing pillar or memorial stone; what Jacob set up at Bethel.
Hebrew mizbeach (H4196) — an altar, literally a place of slaughter; the chief object of this preposition.
Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to dwell or abide; the root of shekinah, the glory that abode on the tabernacle.
Greek epano (G1883) — above, upon; used in Matthew 23:20 of the things upon the altar.
usage: Of consecrating a memorial stone: he poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon (Genesis 35:14).
Of the glory settling on the finished tabernacle: the cloud abode thereon, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35).
Of an oath binding on all that rests upon the altar: sweareth by it, and by all things thereon (Matthew 23:20).
scriptures: Genesis 35:14
And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he talked with him, even a pillar of stone: and he poured a drink offering thereon, and he poured oil thereon.
Exodus 40:35
And Moses was not able to enter into the tent of the congregation, because the cloud abode thereon, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
2 Chronicles 33:16
And he repaired the altar of the LORD, and sacrificed thereon peace offerings and thank offerings, and commanded Judah to serve the LORD God of Israel.
1 Kings 6:35
And he carved thereon cherubims and palm trees and open flowers: and covered them with gold fitted upon the carved work.

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew 'alav and yasaph constructions, Greek pros auto)
etymology: A compound of there and to, meaning to that or to it. In the Authorized Version it appears only nine times, and its weightiest use is in the prohibition against adding to God's word.
biblical_def: Thereto means to it, and its most consequential occurrence is the sentence that closes the second giving of the law: “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). The verse stands at the end of a chapter about worship — where Israel may sacrifice, how she must not enquire after the manner of the nations — and it fences the whole subject. God's word about His own worship is neither to be supplemented nor trimmed. The same formula opens the book at Deuteronomy 4:2 and closes the canon at Revelation 22:18, and Reformed theology has taken it as one of the pillars of the regulative principle of worship: what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted. The word appears elsewhere in the ordinary language of construction and law — a crown of gold made thereto upon the table of shewbread (Exodus 25:24), a fifth part added thereto when a man redeems his tithe (Leviticus 27:31) — where addition is commanded and therefore right.
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning to that or to it. It occurs nine times in the Authorized Version, most weightily in the command that closes Deuteronomy 12 — thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it — a foundation of the regulative principle of worship.
webster_full: THERETO, adv. [there and to.] To that; to this; to it.
2. It refers to a thing before mentioned; as, add thereto.
3. Thereunto is an older and fuller form of the same word.
4. It is retained chiefly in the legal and scriptural style.
5. In Scripture, thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it, Deut. 12; he shall add thereto the fifth part thereof, Lev. 27.
corruption_summary: Worship is now widely governed by what a congregation finds moving rather than by what God has commanded. Deuteronomy's fence cuts both ways: it forbids adding devices God never authorised, and it equally forbids dropping what He did.
corruption_paragraphs: The regulative principle is not a preference for austerity; it is the recognition that God has always reserved the manner of His worship to Himself. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire which he commanded them not, and died for it; Uzzah steadied the ark with the best of intentions and by a means God had forbidden. The 1689 Confession states the rule plainly: the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by Himself and so limited by His own revealed will that He may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men. The question before any element of a service is therefore not whether it works but whether it is commanded.

The prohibition against diminishing is the half more often forgotten. Where Scripture requires the public reading of the word, the preaching of it, prayer, singing, and the two ordinances, a service that has quietly shed most of these has broken the same commandment as one that has added a great deal. Deuteronomy 12:32 is a fence with two rails. The practical test is simple and searching: for each thing done in the assembly, what is the warrant?
roots_summary: Hebrew yasaph is to add or increase, and gara' is to diminish or withdraw; the pair frames the canonical fence. The English adverb joins there to to, answering the Hebrew preposition with a suffix.
roots_lines: Hebrew yasaph (H3254) — to add, to increase, to do again; the forbidden action in Deuteronomy 12:32.
Hebrew gara' (H1639) — to diminish, to withdraw, to take away; the other half of the prohibition.
Hebrew mitzvah (H4687) — a commandment; what may be neither supplemented nor reduced.
Greek epitithemi (G2007) — to add or lay upon; the verb of the warning in Revelation 22:18.
Saxon þærto — the Old English compound of there and to.
usage: Of the fence set about God's commanded worship: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it (Deuteronomy 12:32).
Of an addition God Himself commands: he shall add thereto the fifth part thereof (Leviticus 27:31).
Of ornament appointed for the table of shewbread: make thereto a crown of gold round about (Exodus 25:24).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 12:32
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Deuteronomy 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
Leviticus 27:31
And if a man will at all redeem ought of his tithes, he shall add thereto the fifth part thereof.
Exodus 25:24
And thou shalt overlay it with pure gold, and make thereto a crown of gold round about.

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew bo of means, Greek di' autou)
etymology: A compound of there and by, meaning by that, by means of it, or sometimes near it. English still keeps it in formal prose, where it marks the instrument or the consequence of what has just been said.
biblical_def: Thereby means by that means, and Scripture uses it to fasten a consequence to its cause. Ezekiel states the principle of personal responsibility in its sharpest form: “When the righteous turneth from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, he shall even die thereby” (Ezekiel 33:18) — the death is not arbitrary but is the fruit of the iniquity itself. Ecclesiastes applies the same logic to ordinary labour: “he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby” (Ecclesiastes 10:9), a plain observation that work carries its own risks and wisdom consists partly in knowing them. The word also serves for mere proximity, and there it becomes the language of desolation: Jeremiah says of a doomed city that “every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof” (Jeremiah 19:8), and again that no son of man does “pass thereby” at all (Jeremiah 51:43). A place so wasted that travellers no longer take the road past it is the prophet's picture of judgment complete.
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning by that, by means of it, or near it. In Scripture it ties a consequence to its cause — the man who turns from righteousness shall die thereby — and describes the desolation at which every passer-by is astonished.
webster_full: THEREBY, adv. [there and by.] By that; by means of that; in consequence of that.
2. Near that place; as, he passed thereby.
3. It refers to a cause, an instrument, or a means before mentioned.
4. It is retained in the legal, formal and scriptural style.
5. In Scripture, he shall even die thereby, Ezek. 33; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished, Jer. 19.
corruption_summary: The doctrine of Ezekiel 33 is regularly conscripted for two opposite errors: a works-righteousness that makes standing before God depend on the last thing a man did, and a false assurance that treats a past profession as proof against any present course.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel is addressing the covenant nation and the question of who shall live in the land, and his answer refuses both a hereditary presumption and a merely formal righteousness. But the passage does not overturn justification by faith alone, and it must not be read as though salvation were held on a running tally. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance answers precisely here: those whom God has effectually called and sanctified can neither totally nor finally fall away, but shall certainly persevere to the end. A man who turns from his righteousness and dies thereby demonstrates what his righteousness was, rather than losing a salvation he possessed.

The opposite abuse is more common in evangelical churches and does more harm. A profession made once is treated as a receipt, so that no present course of life can call it into question, and the warnings of Scripture are explained away as hypothetical. But the same confession that denies final apostasy insists that perseverance is the genuine fruit of regeneration and not a bare formula — not once saved, always saved as a slogan detached from a changed life. Ezekiel 33 is preached rightly when it drives the presumptuous to examine themselves and the fearful to Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses means by the preposition be with a suffix, the same form that gives therein; context distinguishes place from instrument. Greek uses dia with the genitive for means and para for proximity.
roots_lines: Hebrew be of instrument — the preposition in used for the means by which a thing is done.
Hebrew 'avon (H5771) — iniquity, guilt, the punishment of iniquity; the thing by which the turner dies.
Hebrew baqa' (H1234) — to cleave or split; the woodcutter's work in Ecclesiastes 10:9.
Greek dia (G1223) — through, by means of; with the genitive, the standard preposition of instrument.
Saxon þærbi — the Old English compound of there and by.
usage: Of a consequence bound to its cause: When the righteous turneth from his righteousness... he shall even die thereby (Ezekiel 33:18).
Of the ordinary risks attending labour: he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby (Ecclesiastes 10:9).
Of a desolation that travellers stop to marvel at: every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished (Jeremiah 19:8).
scriptures: Ezekiel 33:18
When the righteous turneth from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, he shall even die thereby.
Ecclesiastes 10:9
Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby.
Jeremiah 19:8
And I will make this city desolate, and an hissing; every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished and hiss because of all the plagues thereof.
Jeremiah 51:43
Her cities are a desolation, a dry land, and a wilderness, a land wherein no man dwelleth, neither doth any son of man pass thereby.

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew 'asher with a suffix, Greek relative pronouns in the genitive)
etymology: A compound of where and of, meaning of which or of whom. The where- compounds are the relative counterparts of the there- compounds: thereof points back to a thing already named, whereof introduces the clause that describes it.
biblical_def: Whereof means of which, and it does the work of a relative pronoun with a preposition attached. It appears in the LORD's recital of His own commandment in Eden: “the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat” (Genesis 3:11), the clause defining precisely which tree and precisely what was said. Joshua uses it to identify the cities of refuge as a promise already made and now executed: “Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses” (Joshua 20:2). Paul uses it before Felix to demand the ordinary standard of evidence: “Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me” (Acts 24:13) — a Christian appealing, rightly, to Roman rules of proof. And he uses it of his own office: “Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power” (Ephesians 3:7). The psalmist uses it for the river of God: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psalm 46:4).
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning of which or of whom; the relative counterpart of thereof. In Scripture it identifies the thing spoken of — the tree whereof God commanded, the cities whereof He spake, the charges whereof Paul was accused.
webster_full: WHEREOF, adv. [where and of.] Of which; of whom.
2. It introduces a relative clause, and answers to thereof, which refers backward.
3. It belongs to the class of compound relatives: whereof, whereby, wherein, wherewith, whereunto.
4. It is retained chiefly in the legal and scriptural style.
5. In Scripture, the tree, whereof I commanded thee, Gen. 3; the things whereof they now accuse me, Acts 24.
corruption_summary: Paul's demand that his accusers prove their charges is a standing rebuke to accusation by assertion — the trial by reputation that flourishes wherever a claim is treated as established the moment it is made.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the biblical law of witnesses. Scripture requires two or three, provides for the examination of them, and prescribes that a false witness receive the penalty he sought for his brother. Paul stands on this before Felix: neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me. The church has the same rule for its own courts — against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses — a protection that exists precisely because accusations against ministers are easy to make and ruinous to answer.

The rule protects two parties at once, and both halves must be kept. It protects the accused from ruin by rumour; it also requires that credible charges actually be heard, since the same passage that guards the elder commands that those who sin be rebuked before all. A congregation that will not hear evidence against a man it admires has broken the law of witnesses as surely as one that condemns without any. Justice in Scripture is neither indulgent nor credulous; it examines.
roots_summary: Hebrew has one indeclinable relative, 'asher, whose case is supplied by a resumptive pronoun later in the clause; Greek declines its relative hos and puts it in the genitive for whereof.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asher (H834) — who, which, that; an indeclinable relative whose sense is fixed by the clause.
Greek hou (G3739) — of which or of whom; the genitive of the relative pronoun.
Greek apodeiknumi (G584) — to prove or demonstrate; the verb Paul's accusers could not satisfy.
Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge or asylum; the cities appointed in Joshua 20:2.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant or minister; what Paul was made of the gospel in Ephesians 3:7.
usage: Of the precise commandment recalled in Eden: the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat (Genesis 3:11).
Of a promise now being executed: cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses (Joshua 20:2).
Of charges that could not be proved: Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me (Acts 24:13).
scriptures: Genesis 3:11
And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?
Joshua 20:2
Speak to the children of Israel, saying, Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses:
Acts 24:13
Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me.
Ephesians 3:7
Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power.

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew bammah and 'asher with be, Greek en ho and di' hou)
etymology: A compound of where and by, meaning by which or by what means. It serves both as a relative (the means whereby) and as an interrogative (whereby shall I know?).
biblical_def: Whereby asks or names the means. Abram, having just been counted righteous by faith, asks for a sign concerning the land: “Lord GOD, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it?” (Genesis 15:8), and God answers not with a rebuke but with a covenant ceremony in which He alone passes between the pieces. The question is the honest one of a believing man asking how he may know, and Scripture treats it as such. As a relative the word names the instrument of mercy: “Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us” (Luke 1:78), where Zacharias traces the incarnation itself to the mercy of God as its cause. It can also name a means of judgment: the LORD says through Ezekiel that He gave a rebellious people “statutes that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live” (Ezekiel 20:25) — a judicial handing over to what they had chosen. And it serves in plain narrative and civic speech alike, from Jonathan's reading of his father's intent (1 Samuel 20:33) to the Ephesian town clerk dispersing a riot (Acts 19:40).
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning by which or by what means; both relative and interrogative. In Scripture it frames Abram's honest request for assurance, the mercy whereby the dayspring visited us, and the judgments whereby a rebellious people should not live.
webster_full: WHEREBY, adv. [where and by.] By which; by what means.
2. Interrogatively, by what? as, whereby shall I know this?
3. It is the relative counterpart of thereby, which refers backward.
4. It is retained chiefly in the legal, formal and scriptural style.
5. In Scripture, whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it? Gen. 15; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, Luke 1.
corruption_summary: Asking God for assurance is often treated as unbelief, and assurance itself is often reduced to a feeling. Scripture shows a justified man asking whereby shall I know and receiving an answer, and it names the grounds on which a believer may know.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 15 is the decisive case. Abram believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness; two verses later he asks how he shall know that he will inherit the land. God does not treat the question as a lapse. He commands a covenant sacrifice, and then, in the deep sleep and the horror of great darkness, passes between the pieces alone — taking the self-maledictory oath upon Himself while Abram does nothing. The assurance given is not a feeling produced but a promise sworn, and the whole of Hebrews 6 reasons from this scene to the strong consolation of those who have fled for refuge.

The Reformed confessions guard the doctrine on both sides. Assurance is not of the essence of faith, so that a true believer may wait long and wrestle with many difficulties before he attain it; and yet it may, without extraordinary revelation, be certainly attained, being founded on the divine truth of the promises, the inward evidence of the graces to which those promises are made, and the testimony of the Spirit of adoption. So a Christian who lacks assurance is not therefore lost, and one who has it has more than an impression. The question whereby shall I know has an answer, and the answer is not taken from within.
roots_summary: Hebrew asks bammah, by what, and relates by 'asher with the preposition be; Greek uses en ho or dia with the relative in the genitive. The vocabulary of covenant sign and oath governs the key texts.
roots_lines: Hebrew bammah (H4100) — by what, wherewith; the interrogative of means in Abram's question.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant; God's answer to the request for assurance in Genesis 15.
Greek anatole (G395) — a rising, the dayspring; the sunrise figure of Luke 1:78 for the incarnate Christ.
Greek splagchna eleous (G4698, G1656) — bowels of mercy, tender mercy; the cause named by Zacharias.
Greek en ho (G1722, G3739) — in or by which; the standard construction rendered whereby.
usage: Of a believer asking for assurance and receiving a covenant: whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it? (Genesis 15:8).
Of the mercy that produced the incarnation: whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us (Luke 1:78).
Of a judicial handing-over to chosen statutes: judgments whereby they should not live (Ezekiel 20:25).

Luke 1:78

Ezekiel 20:25

1 Samuel 20:33

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew 'asher... shammah, Greek eis ho)
etymology: A compound of where and unto, meaning to which or unto what. It is the fuller and older form answering to thereunto, and in the epistles it becomes a word of vocation — the end to which a man is called and toward which he labours.
biblical_def: Whereunto means to which, and in the New Testament it repeatedly marks a calling and its object. Paul charges Timothy: “Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1 Timothy 6:12). Eternal life is not merely offered but is the end to which the man was called, and the fight is the taking hold of what God has already appointed. Of his own ministry he says, “Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily” (Colossians 1:29) — a sentence that holds together the hardest human effort and the divine energy producing it, which is the Reformed account of sanctification in miniature. The word also frames the Lord's search for a fit comparison: “Whereunto then shall I liken the men of this generation?” (Luke 7:31). And the psalmist uses it of God as a place of continual return: “Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort” (Psalm 71:3).
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning to which or unto what. In Scripture it names the end to which a man is called — eternal life, whereunto thou art also called — and the labour undertaken toward it.
webster_full: WHEREUNTO, adv. [where and unto.] To which; unto which; to what end.
2. Interrogatively, to what? as, whereunto shall I liken it?
3. It is the fuller form of whereto, and answers to thereunto, which refers backward.
4. It is retained chiefly in the scriptural and formal style.
5. In Scripture, eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, 1 Tim. 6; Whereunto I also labour, Col. 1.
corruption_summary: Calling has been thinned into career language — a personal sense of fit, a passion to be followed. In Scripture the calling is God's act with an object He has named, and the believer's part is to lay hold of what he was called to.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is effectual calling as God's work. In the New Testament the called are those whom God has summoned out of darkness, and the calling is according to His purpose and grace, given in Christ before the world began. Vocation in the Reformation sense then follows: because God has called a man to Himself, the ordinary work of his hands is service rendered to God and not a lesser thing than ministry. Luther and the Puritans recovered exactly this against a medieval scheme that reserved vocation for monks and priests.

Colossians 1:29 keeps the balance the doctrine needs. Paul labours — the verb is one of agony and exhaustion — and he labours according to his working, which worketh in me mightily. Sanctification is neither passive waiting nor unaided effort. It is real striving, empowered by real grace, and the same apostle who says work out your own salvation with fear and trembling gives the reason in the next breath: for it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. A calling in Scripture always comes with the power to pursue it.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses whereunto with the relative 'asher and a directional suffix; Greek uses eis ho or the dative of the relative. The vocabulary of calling — kaleo, klesis — governs the New Testament texts.
roots_lines: Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call, to summon, to name; the verb of God's effectual calling.
Greek klesis (G2821) — a calling or invitation; the noun for the vocation to which believers are summoned.
Greek agonizomai (G75) — to strive as in a contest, to agonize; Paul's labour in Colossians 1:29.
Greek energeia (G1753) — working, operative power; the divine energy at work in that labour.
Hebrew ma'on (H4583) — a habitation or dwelling; the strong habitation of Psalm 71:3.
usage: Of the end to which a believer is called: eternal life, whereunto thou art also called (1 Timothy 6:12).
Of labour empowered by God's own working: Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working (Colossians 1:29).
Of God as a refuge continually returned to: Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort (Psalm 71:3).

Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew bammah and 'asher... bo, Greek en ho)
etymology: A compound of where and in, meaning in which or in what. As an interrogative it asks in what respect a thing is so, and Malachi has made that use famous: seven times a rebuked people answer the prophet with the single word Wherein?
biblical_def: Wherein asks or names the respect in which something holds. Its most striking use in Scripture is Malachi's, where a people under rebuke answer every charge with a question. The LORD says they have despised His name; they reply, “Wherein have we despised thy name?” He says they have polluted His altar; they reply, “Wherein have we polluted thee?” (Malachi 1:7). The pattern repeats through the book — wherein have we wearied him, wherein shall we return, wherein have we robbed thee — and it is not honest enquiry but self-defence dressed as enquiry. Each time the LORD answers with a specific, unanswerable particular: the blind and lame animals brought for sacrifice, the tithes withheld. The word serves elsewhere for the plain respect in which a thing is true: the creatures entering the ark, “wherein is the breath of life” (Genesis 7:15); the leper's days “wherein the plague shall be in him” (Leviticus 13:46); and Rabshakeh's taunt at the wall of Jerusalem, “What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?” (2 Kings 18:19), which is the right question asked by the wrong man.
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning in which or in what respect. In Scripture it is the word of Malachi's self-justifying congregation — Wherein have we polluted thee? — and of Rabshakeh's taunt, What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?
webster_full: WHEREIN, adv. [where and in.] In which; in what; in what respect.
2. Interrogatively, in what? as, wherein have I offended?
3. It is the relative counterpart of therein, which refers backward.
4. It is retained chiefly in the scriptural and formal style.
5. In Scripture, Wherein have we polluted thee? Mal. 1; What confidence is this wherein thou trustest? 2 Kings 18.
corruption_summary: Malachi's Wherein? is the perfect specimen of a conscience that answers every charge with a demand for particulars in order to avoid the charge itself. It is alive in every congregation, and it is defeated the same way the prophet defeats it: by naming the particular.
corruption_paragraphs: The men of Malachi's day were not irreligious. They kept a temple, maintained a priesthood, and offered sacrifices; what they brought were the animals nobody wanted — the blind, the lame, the sick — and they could not see that this despised anything. Hence the repeated Wherein? It is the reflex of a religion that has become formal, where the outward acts continue and the heart has quietly withdrawn, and where the man himself is the last to notice. The prophet's method is the remedy: not a general appeal to sincerity but a specific fact laid on the table. Offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee?

Rabshakeh's taunt is the same question in an enemy's mouth, and it is worth facing. What confidence is this wherein thou trustest? The Assyrian meant it as mockery, and he was wrong about the answer, but the question is one every believer should be able to answer plainly. Hezekiah's reply was to spread the letter before the LORD, which is the model: the confidence is not in the walls, nor in Egypt, nor in the king's resources, but in the God who made heaven and earth. A faith that cannot say wherein it trusts, when an enemy asks, has not yet been examined.
roots_summary: Hebrew asks bammah, in what; the relative sense uses 'asher with the preposition be and a resumptive pronoun. Greek uses en ho and en tini. Malachi's disputation form is built entirely on this interrogative.
roots_lines: Hebrew bammah (H4100) — in what, wherein; the interrogative repeated seven times in Malachi.
Hebrew ga'al (H1351) — to pollute or defile; the charge the priests could not see in Malachi 1:7.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to be confident; the verb of Rabshakeh's taunt.
Hebrew bittachon (H986) — confidence, trust; the noun in what confidence is this.
Greek en tini (G1722, G5101) — in what; the Greek interrogative answering to wherein.
usage: Of a rebuked people demanding particulars to evade the charge: Wherein have we polluted thee? (Malachi 1:7).
Of the question every believer should be able to answer: What confidence is this wherein thou trustest? (2 Kings 18:19).
Of the plain respect in which a thing is true: all flesh, wherein is the breath of life (Genesis 7:15).

pos: adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew bammah, Greek en ho and the dative of instrument)
etymology: A compound of where and with, meaning with which or with what. It names the instrument or accompaniment, and as an interrogative it asks what a man has to bring.
biblical_def: Wherewith asks or names what a thing is done with. Micah puts the great question of all religion in exactly this form: “Wherewith shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old?” (Micah 6:6). The escalation that follows — thousands of rams, ten thousands of rivers of oil, the firstborn for the sin of the soul — is the sound of a man discovering that there is no quantity of anything that will answer. The prophet's reply strips the question down: to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God. The word carries other weights. It names oppression measured by its instrument: “I have also seen the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress them” (Exodus 3:9). It names a blessing by its author: “this is the blessing, wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death” (Deuteronomy 33:1). And Paul uses it to define the whole business of Christians with one another: “things wherewith one may edify another” (Romans 14:19).
webster_summary: A compound adverb meaning with which or with what; naming the instrument or the means. In Scripture it frames Micah's question — wherewith shall I come before the LORD? — and Paul's rule that Christians pursue the things wherewith one may edify another.
webster_full: WHEREWITH, adv. [where and with.] With which; with what.
2. Interrogatively, with what? as, wherewith shall I come?
3. It is the relative counterpart of therewith, which refers backward.
4. Wherewithal is a strengthened form of the same word.
5. In Scripture, Wherewith shall I come before the LORD? Micah 6; things wherewith one may edify another, Rom. 14.
corruption_summary: Micah's question is the question of every religion of works, and the escalating offers show where it ends — in a bidding war a sinner cannot win. The gospel answers it not by lowering the price but by naming the one who paid it.
corruption_paragraphs: The offers in Micah 6:6-7 rise deliberately from the reasonable to the monstrous: yearling calves, then thousands of rams, then ten thousand rivers of oil, then a man's own firstborn. That last suggestion is not piety but pagan logic, and Scripture condemns it absolutely; that a worshipper should even think of it shows how the works principle drives a guilty conscience. Every system of merit — the treasury of merit and indulgences of medieval Rome, the modern hope of outweighing one's failures with good intentions — is a variation on this bidding, and the answer is always the same: nothing brought will be enough, because the debt is not quantitative.

Micah's reply is not a lighter law but a truer one, and it exposes rather than relieves: to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God is more than sacrifices, not less. What the prophet requires, no man has done. So the question stands open until the New Testament answers it — ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold... but with the precious blood of Christ. That is the true wherewith: not what the sinner brings, but what the Substitute brought. And the Christian's doing justly and loving mercy then follows as gratitude rather than as payment.
roots_summary: Hebrew bammah asks with what; the relative sense uses 'asher with the instrumental be. Greek uses the dative of instrument or en ho. The vocabulary of sacrifice and of edification governs the key texts.
roots_lines: Hebrew bammah (H4100) — with what, wherewith; the interrogative of Micah 6:6.
Hebrew 'olah (H5930) — a burnt offering, that which ascends; the first thing offered in Micah's escalation.
Hebrew lachats (H3906) — oppression, distress; the instrument of Egyptian cruelty in Exodus 3:9.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — building up, edification; the aim of Christian conduct in Romans 14:19.
Greek dative of instrument — the case expressing the means by which an action is performed.
usage: Of the question every religion of works must ask: Wherewith shall I come before the LORD? (Micah 6:6).
Of oppression named by its instrument: the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress them (Exodus 3:9).
Of the rule for Christian conduct toward one another: things wherewith one may edify another (Romans 14:19).
